summary: The article discusses rising greenhouse gas emissions from local urban transport, centered on a February 2024 study by Dr. Emily Nguyen's team at the City University Environmental Research Group. It finds transport accounts for about 30% of city GHG emissions, with personal vehicles the dominant source, and public transport also hampered by inefficiency. It covers growth in electric mobility, low uptake of active travel, and policy and technology recommendations for sustainable transport.
one_line: A February 2024 city study by Dr. Emily Nguyen finds local transport causes about 30% of GHG emissions and proposes EV, transit and active-travel policies.
key_facts: A study released in February 2024, led by Dr. Emily Nguyen of the City University Environmental Research Group, found local transportation contributed approximately 30% of the city's total GHG emissions.
The study analyzed vehicle emissions, fuel types, public transit efficiency, and active travel (cycling, walking) statistics.
In November 2023, 65% of all local transport emissions stemmed from personal vehicle use, according to the study.
An audit of the local bus fleet in October 2023 found more than half of the buses operating at suboptimal levels of fuel efficiency and emissions output.
Electric vehicle sales soared in 2023, and EV infrastructure such as charging stations expanded significantly by January 2024.
The Electric Transport Coalition, led by activist James Carter, reported a 40% increase in public EV charging stations in the city since September 2023.
The study notes that EV benefits are undercut if the electricity used originates from fossil fuels, so clean energy generation must support the transition.
A survey in the study found only 15% of local residents chose cycling or walking over short distances.

Dr. Nguyen's policy recommendations include expanding EV purchase incentives, upgrading public transit fleets to greener technologies, and investing in urban planning that prioritizes pedestrian and cycling networks.
Dr. Nguyen said, "The convenience of personal vehicles comes at an environmental cost."
The article advocates a multi-stakeholder approach involving lawmakers, industry, and the community, with public participation in policy formation.
Emerging solutions highlighted include autonomous vehicles, smart traffic management systems, and integration of renewable energy sources.
